text: You can now pull Sentinel incidents and AWS Security Hub findings on their own. This lesson puts both halves of the chapter together -- a real Python script that normalizes both into one shape and correlates them, answering a question neither cloud can answer by itself.

Sentinel incidents nest their related entities under properties. ASFF findings nest their IP addresses under resources and details. Before you can compare anything, both need to land in one common record -- just a source tag, an ID, a severity, and the set of IPs or usernames the item touched. That shared shape is what makes correlation logic possible at all.

Each normalize function absorbs the messiness of its own schema and hands back the same flat dictionary. The Sentinel version loops related entities checking for kind equals IP. The ASFF version loops resources, drills into the EC2 instance details, and collects every IPv4 address it finds. Neither function needs to know anything about the other cloud -- it only needs to produce the agreed-upon shape.

With both sources normalized, correlation is just a set intersection. For every Sentinel item and every AWS item, check whether their IP sets overlap. If they do, that's a match -- record both IDs and the shared IPs. No fuzzy matching, no machine learning, just checking whether the same concrete value shows up on both sides. The same pattern extends to usernames or resource IDs by intersecting a different field.

Notice what this script deliberately does not do. It doesn't close the Sentinel incident. It doesn't isolate the EC2 instance. It doesn't block the IP anywhere. It produces a list of correlated pairs with both severities and both IDs attached, so an analyst can decide whether this is one attacker visible from two clouds, or just a coincidence.

That's automate the pipeline, gate the action, from Chapter 1, made concrete: Python normalizes two schemas and intersects sets across potentially thousands of records, and a human makes the call on what the match actually means. Chapter 3 picks this up from here, turning scripts like this one into real, gated SOAR playbooks.
